ordered_diagnoses: Brain abscess due to Toxoplasma or Nocardia

facts.raw_span: A 19-year-old man with hepatitis C and intravenous heroin use
altered mental status
febrile and intermittently responsive (Glasgow Coma Scale 10)
left upper- and lower-limb weakness (strength 2/5 and 3/5)
leukocytosis (white blood cell count rising from 10.0 to 14.6 × 10^3/µL)
Urine toxicology was positive for benzodiazepines and opiates
Noncontrast head CT demonstrated a hypodense area in the right basal ganglia with mass effect but no hemorrhage
Brain MRI revealed T2/FLAIR hyperintensity in the right basal ganglia and internal capsule with mild surrounding edema
Lumbar puncture yielded an opening pressure of 23 cm H₂O and slightly hazy cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) with 538 WBCs/mm³
no valvular vegetations
Repeat lumbar puncture showed an opening pressure of 30 cm H₂O, 1762 WBCs/mm³
Repeat MRI demonstrated progression with new involvement of the left basal ganglia, increased diffusion restriction, development of necrosis, and new peripheral contrast enhancement

concepts.why: The patient's symptoms and imaging findings, including hypodense areas in the basal ganglia and T2/FLAIR hyperintensity, are consistent with cerebral toxoplasmosis, particularly in the context of his immunocompromised state due to hepatitis C and intravenous heroin use.

The patient's fever, leukocytosis, and imaging findings, including a hypodense area with mass effect, are consistent with a pyogenic brain abscess, which could be related to his intravenous heroin use and potential for bacteremia.

The patient's immunocompromised state and imaging findings, including T2/FLAIR hyperintensity and progression with new involvement of the left basal ganglia, are consistent with progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy, a rare and often fatal demyelinating disease caused by the JC virus.

The patient's symptoms, including limb weakness and altered mental status, and imaging findings, including hypodense areas in the basal ganglia and progression with new involvement of the left basal ganglia, are consistent with CNS vasculitis, which could be related to his hepatitis C or other underlying conditions.

The patient's fever, leukocytosis, and positive urine toxicology for benzodiazepines and opiates, which may indicate intravenous drug use and increased risk for endocarditis, are consistent with subacute bacterial endocarditis, although the absence of valvular vegetations on echocardiography makes this diagnosis less likely.

The patient's immunocompromised state and imaging findings, including hypodense areas in the basal ganglia and progression with new involvement of the left basal ganglia, are consistent with a fungal brain abscess, which could be related to his intravenous heroin use and potential for fungal infections.
The patient's fever, altered mental status, and leukocytosis are consistent with a rickettsial disease, although the negative rickettsial studies make this diagnosis less likely.

The patient's altered mental status, fever, and imaging findings, including T2/FLAIR hyperintensity in the basal ganglia, are consistent with herpes simplex encephalitis, although the negative herpes simplex virus PCR makes this diagnosis less likely.

The patient's symptoms, including limb weakness and altered mental status, and imaging findings, including hypodense areas in the basal ganglia, are consistent with CNS tuberculosis, which could be related to his immunocompromised state due to hepatitis C and intravenous heroin use.

rationales.F07: The presence of a hypodense area in the right basal ganglia with mass effect on head CT is suggestive of a focal brain lesion, which could be consistent with cerebral toxoplasmosis, pyogenic brain abscess, or fungal brain abscess.
rationales.F08: The T2/FLAIR hyperintensity in the right basal ganglia and internal capsule with mild surrounding edema on brain MRI is consistent with a focal brain infection or inflammation, which could be seen in cerebral toxoplasmosis, pyogenic brain abscess, or fungal brain abscess.
